reporting-org.narrative: Defence for Children International Netherlands - ECPAT Netherlands

description.narrative: Sexual exploitation of children (SEC) is a grave violation of children’s rights and affects millions of children and youth annually, regardless of gender. No region, country or child is immune, though girls, boys and children with other gender identities face differing levels of risk to different manifestations of SEC depending on their intersectional vulnerability factors. It impacts heavily and long lastingly on their physical, emotional and mental well-being. It deprives children and youth of establishing healthy (sexual) relationships and from developing to the best of their potential. The SUFASEC programme is designed to combat SEC and will work in 12 countries in Latin America and South and South East Asia: Bangladesh, Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Dominican Republic, Guatemala, India, Indonesia, Laos, Nepal, Philippines and Thailand.

The SUFASEC programme is designed to combat SEC by working towards the following long-term impact: “Children in all of their diversity are better protected from sexual exploitation.” This activity forms part of the SUFASEC programme. The long-term impact will be reached through three interlinking objectives that address different dimensions (social norms, assets/environments, and laws/policies/systems). 1. Children, youth and their communities successfully challenge social norms and harmful practices related to SEC 2. Children and youth have access to and are supported by strengthened assets and protective environments 3. Children and civil society meaningfully participate in holding duty bearers, including government and local authorities, accountable to their obligations towards improved (implementation of) laws, policies, and systems.

The different stakeholder groups involved in the SUFASEC programme include: - Children and youth in all their diversity: A child-centred approach: children and youth are the most important stakeholders. When children/youth fall victim to SEC the physical and mental impact can be long lasting. The Alliance adheres to the UN definition of child (0-18 years) and youth (15-24 years) - Caregivers and Communities: Critical stakeholders in the community include parents, caregivers, community leaders, teachers, local Community Based Organisations (CBOs), social workers, and other community members involved in community based child protection mechanisms. - CSOs and CBOs: Local child protection organisations support and implement activities at community level, L&A towards national actors, and provide synergies of interventions. - Local and national governments: formulate, endorse and implement laws and public policies related to SEC - Private Sector: Travel and tourism orgs (e.g., large and small, hotels, transport), as well as ICT/ Digital Service Providers have interest to avoid SEC taking place within their value chain, and to avoid having their products and services used to facilitate SEC - International donors, Intergovernmental bodies, INGOs, Multilateral entities55: Targeted audiences and partners for evidence based regional and international lobbying - Dutch Stakeholders: NL Embassies in programme countries, MoFA, MoJ&S, to formalise the network for sustainable cooperation to end SEC and impunity of offenders. The Dutch Public - Media & Journalists: Investigative and reporting outlets in the Programme countries. Media and journalists in the Netherlands.

comment.narrative: This indicator includes young people reached with information on SEC (and not only SRH). Age range: 12-16 y.o. In this indicator, there are two modules provided to the target group. The first module focuses on Gender-Based Violence (Gender, SOGIE), UNCRC and HR, and Sexual Exploitation of Children (Forms and Red Flags) and where to report different types of exploitation. The second module comprises topics about SRHR such as Healthy Body Image, Good and Bad Touch, Pregnancy & Parenthood, Reproductive Health & Services, Safe sex and contraception, Consent & Healthy Relationships, Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights

A total of 731 children, consisting of 424 females, 307 males, and 11 others, were provided with comprehensive and accurate information on Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights (SRHR) and Sexual Exploitation of Children (SEC) from three Secondary High Schools in Boracay Island and 1 elementary, and two Secondary High Schools in Baclayon, Bohol. These awareness activities were conducted from September 2023 to February 2024, and the participating schools were selected as part of the SUFASEC Project. The project prioritized grade 7 students as participants since most in this age group are at the onset of adolescence stage. The response has been remarkable, with many schools requesting to include all Grade 7 students in the activities instead of just a selected few, leading to a significant increase in the number of children reached.Activities: School Education Awareness and Peer-to-peer

title.narrative: # of CSOs (not youth or women led) with increased L&A capacities

comment.narrative: The organization faces significant challenges due to a lack of capacity and strategic planning in integrating Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights (SRHR) into efforts against Sexual Exploitation of Children (SEC). Furthermore, there is a shortage of materials and resources for conducting effective educational awareness campaigns on SRHR.

The desired activities prioritize engaging in dialogues and consultations with both government and private stakeholders who possess the necessary capacity and knowledge regarding their existing materials and resources relevant to the project. This includes crafting a specific module tailored for the SUFASEC Project, seamlessly integrating Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights (SRHR) with efforts against Sexual Exploitation of Children (SEC).Additionally, conducting workshops and capacity training sessions for the organization based on the outcomes of these modules is essential for continuous improvement and effective implementation of the project's objectives.

ECPAT Philippines' staff organized a Project Development Workshop from June 6 to 9, 2023, in Malay, Aklan. The workshop centered around a team-building exercise aimed at equipping all staff with the necessary knowledge and skills for the new SUFASEC project. The main objectives of the capacity-building workshop were as follows: 1. Demonstrate a comprehensive understanding of ECPAT Philippines' SUFASEC project; 2. Explain the key features of the newly developed modules designed to achieve essential SUFASEC outcomes for its beneficiaries; 3. Conduct simulated module sessions for school children and the private sector, targeting effective engagement; 4. Evaluate the module content and methodology based on the specified objectives; 5. Identify critical areas for improvement and outline the next steps for refining the draft modules for both school children and the private sector. Following the workshop, significant enhancements were made to the modules used in the implementation of the SUFASEC project. These improvements were then applied effectively to targeted sectors, including Civil Society Organizations (CSOs) within the Tourism Industry and local communities. Tourism Frontliners such as tourguides, tourdrivers, hotel personnel, and community leaders were trained and provided awareness on SEC and SRHR. An invitation for awareness training on SECTT for Boracay Island tourism frontliners and community members on November 30, 2023, was unexpectedly well attended by 17 tourism-related associations, representing each particular sector. They are boatmen, island hopping operators, travel agencies, photographers, tour guides, paraw boat operators, parasailing groups, hotel and resort associations, massage therapist associations, fire dancers, hair braiders associations, and land transportation groups.
